The Verilog fact is true: in a four-state run an if on `r != 0` with r unknown takes the else branch, `r !== 0` takes the then branch, and `r == 0` takes the else branch (Icarus Verilog, run by the checker). No source page states it; the document says so by marking it inference.

[CIP], 'writing 0 changes nothing' (line 65): the page says the event is acknowledged by writing 1 to a write-1-to-clear field and does not say in words what a 0 does; [PIC] line 'ignore any write otherwise' does. The reading is fair; the tag is [CIP] alone.

[CIP] [PIC], 'An event lost when it lands on the cycle of a clear' (line 88), carries source tags and no inference mark. Neither page names this failure: [CIP] says a clear with the event still active returns the bit to true, and [PIC] writes the next status as new events OR (old AND NOT written bits) with the comment 'only if the interrupt source is also inactive'. The failure is the contrapositive of both. It should read as inference at the document's next edit; the sentence is true.

[GPIO] filter (lines 41-42): the page calls it an optional 16-cycle noise filter per input, applied to both DATA_IN and interrupt detection; 'waits for a stable value' is the document's description of what such a filter does.

[CDC] (lines 38-40): the two-flip-flop method, 'some even recommend three', and 'none of your code should reference the output of the flip-flops in the metastable region' are on the page. The page gives the method for a value from another clock domain and adds that it works when the value changes much more slowly than the new clock; the document applies it to a pin without that caveat, which is the document's extension (a pin is an asynchronous input).

[CIP] and [GPIO] on the output (line 69-70): the page says INTR_STATE is not qualified by INTR_ENABLE and that the output is the state after masking (ANDing) with INTR_ENABLE; all wired interrupts are active-high level-triggered.
